# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Crop Production
Description: The USDA Crop Production report, released monthly by the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), provides official estimates on U.S. agricultural acreage, yield, and production for major field crops, fruits, and nuts.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset thoroughly, verifying the details you provided and digging into the publisher, legal authority, history, users, and public benefits.Two final rounds of research—on data access/preservation and on recent threats and advocacy concerns.I've gathered comprehensive, verified information. Note: one of my searches hit a result cap, so I've flagged a few recent developments as "verify independently" where I couldn't confirm them with a source. Here is the full report.

---

# Research Report: USDA "Crop Production" Report (NASS)

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your description is **accurate**, with two refinements worth noting:

- ✅ **Title**: "Crop Production" — correct.
- ✅ **Publisher**: Released monthly by the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), USDA — correct. More precisely, it is issued by the **Agricultural Statistics Board (ASB)**, the official estimating body within NASS.
- ✅ **Content**: Official estimates of U.S. acreage, yield, and production — correct. However, the coverage is slightly different from "major field crops, fruits, and nuts" in emphasis: the monthly report's core forecasts center on **corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, rice, sorghum, sugar crops, peanuts, citrus and other fruits, nuts, and hops**, plus specialty items like maple syrup. Livestock products (e.g., milk, honey) are largely covered in *separate* NASS reports.
- ⚠️ **Nuance**: Not every month's report covers every crop. Forecasts follow the growing season (e.g., winter wheat forecasts begin in May; corn/soybean forecasts run August–November; the January issue serves as the annual "final" summary).

---

## 2. Publisher and Institutional Context

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Issuing agency | National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), USDA |
| Authorizing body on reports | Agricultural Statistics Board (ASB) |
| Parent mission area | Research, Education, and Economics (REE), USDA |
| Release schedule | Monthly, typically between the 9th–12th, at 12:00 noon ET |
| Contact | nass@usda.gov; 800-727-9540 |

NASS issues roughly **300 national and 9,000 state-level reports annually** covering 150+ commodities; Crop Production is one of its flagship "principal economic indicator"-class releases and is among the most market-sensitive documents the federal government publishes.

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

The report does not stem from a single statute but from a layered legal foundation:

1. **Organic Act of 1862** — The Act creating USDA (signed by Lincoln) listed gathering and disseminating agricultural statistics as the Department's first duty.
2. **Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (7 U.S.C. §§ 1621–1627)** — NASS's broad operating authority for data collection and dissemination.
3. **7 U.S.C. § 2204(a)** — General authority of the Secretary of Agriculture to collect and publish statistics; cited in NASS's Paperwork Reduction Act notices as the collection authority for the underlying surveys.
4. **Commodity-specific statutes** — e.g., cotton (7 U.S.C. § 476), peanuts (7 U.S.C. § 951), apples (7 U.S.C. § 411b), commodity reports (7 U.S.C. § 1421d).
5. **Delegation of authority** — 7 CFR § 2.68 formally delegates to the NASS Administrator the duty to "prepare crop and livestock estimates… Prepare reports of the Agricultural Statistics Board."
6. **Census of Agriculture Act of 1997 (P.L. 105-113; 7 U.S.C. § 2204g)** — Governs the quinquennial Census of Agriculture, which provides the benchmarks against which Crop Production survey estimates are calibrated.

**Confidentiality framework (important for data librarians and respondents):**
- **CIPSEA (Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act, Title III of P.L. 115-435)** — Individual responses are confidential and usable only for statistical purposes.
- **7 U.S.C. § 2276** (Food Security Act of 1985, § 1770) — Requires strict confidentiality of non-aggregated data.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act** — All surveys carry OMB control numbers and published burden estimates.

---

## 4. History

The Crop Production report is one of the **oldest continuously published federal statistical series in the United States**:

- **1862** — USDA established; statistics-gathering is its first enumerated duty.
- **July 10, 1863** — First monthly crop condition report issued, with a promise of a report "on the tenth of every month" — the direct ancestor of today's Crop Production report. (Civil War supply logistics and correcting farmers' information disadvantage versus commodity buyers were early motivations.)
- **1905** — Crop Reporting Board created (now the Agricultural Statistics Board) to reconcile state and national estimates into official figures.
- **1914–1986** — Organizational lineage (per National Archives Record Group 355): Bureau of Crop Estimates (1914–21) → Bureau of Agricultural Economics (1922–53) → Statistical Reporting Service (1961–77, 1981–86) → renamed **NASS in 1986** (Secretary's Memorandum 1020-24).
- **Methodological evolution** — From subjective reports by volunteer crop correspondents (19th century) to probability-based sampling: list-frame and area-frame surveys, **Objective Yield Surveys** (physical counts/measurements in randomly selected fields for corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, citrus, and tree nuts), farmer-reported acreage surveys, and increasing use of remote sensing and administrative data (e.g., FSA acreage certifications).
- **Release-time history** — Reports were released at 3:00 p.m. ET before May 1994; moved to 8:30 a.m. ET (1994), then to **12:00 noon ET (January 2013)**.
- **2018 reform** — After determining that media receiving reports ~90 minutes early in "lockup" gained a technological market advantage, USDA (with CFTC input) ended early media access; since August 1, 2018, *everyone* receives the report simultaneously at noon.

This lineage matters to preservationists: the series has near-continuous coverage for 160+ years, but under changing agency names, report titles, and methodologies.

---

## 5. Production Process: The "Lockup" and the Agricultural Statistics Board

The report's integrity procedures are remarkable and worth documenting:

- Forecasts for corn, wheat, cotton, soybeans, and oranges are **"speculative" commodities by law** because they are traded on futures markets; early access would confer a trading advantage.
- State field offices transmit **encrypted** estimates to headquarters; files are locked in safes and purged from systems until lockup begins.
- Before release, the ASB convenes in a physically secured room: doors locked and guarded, windows sealed with tamper-resistant shades, phones and internet disconnected, cell phones surrendered, and the area swept for transmissions. **Not even the Secretary of Agriculture** sees the numbers before entering lockup to sign the report.
- Crop Production is **prepared jointly with the WASDE report** (World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates, issued by the World Agricultural Outlook Board) so that NASS production forecasts feed directly into USDA's official supply/demand balance sheets. All USDA agencies' country-level numbers must be consistent with these figures.

---

## 6. Data Contents, Formats, and Access Points

### What's in the report
- U.S. and state-level **planted/harvested acreage, yield, and production** forecasts and estimates
- Crops: corn, soybeans, all wheat (winter/durum/spring by class), cotton, rice, sorghum, barley, oats, sugarbeets/sugarcane, peanuts, tobacco, dry beans/peas, lentils, chickpeas, potatoes, citrus (oranges, grapefruit, lemons), noncitrus fruits, tree nuts (almonds, walnuts, pecans, hazelnuts, pistachios), hops, maple syrup
- Monthly weather and agricultural summaries; methodology and revision notes

### Access channels (key for data librarians and scientists)
| Channel | What it offers |
|---|---|
| **NASS website** (nass.usda.gov/Publications) | Current PDF, TXT, and ZIP of each release |
| **Quick Stats** (quickstats.nass.usda.gov) | Queryable database of the underlying statistics — national, state, county; downloadable CSV |
| **Quick Stats API** | Free API key; JSON/XML/CSV; 50,000 records/call; robust client libraries exist (R: `rnassqs`; Python: `nasspython`) |
| **Bulk data files** | Full Quick Stats database as compressed .txt.gz dumps, updated daily |
| **ESMIS / National Agricultural Library** (esmis.nal.usda.gov) | Archive of releases (PDF/TXT/ZIP) with a documented **public REST API** (OpenAPI spec available) |
| **Cornell Mann Library** (usda.library.cornell.edu) | Long-standing third-party archival mirror of USDA reports, including deep historical runs |

### Data characteristics for data scientists
- Published as **forecasts, estimates, and revisions** — a single month can be re-estimated multiple times; **vintage matters**. Reproducible research must record which release (vintage) was used; the bulk files and Quick Stats preserve "reference period" and revision flags.
- Units vary (bushels, hundredweight, 480-lb bales, pounds, tons); suppression codes protect confidentiality at fine geographies.
- The series is **public domain** (U.S. government work), enabling unrestricted reuse and third-party redistribution.

---

## 7. Typical Users

- **Commodity markets and traders** — The report is genuinely *market-moving*; NASS itself publishes a companion study, "Price Reactions After USDA Crop Reports," documenting price responses for corn, soybeans, wheat, and cotton.
- **Farmers and ranchers** — Marketing and planting decisions; NASS's founding rationale was to equalize information between farmers and buyers.
- **USDA agencies** — WAOB (WASDE), FAS, ERS, and Farm Service Agency all build on these numbers.
- **Policy makers** — Farm bill design, crop insurance (RMA), farm program payment rates, disaster assistance triggers, and CBO baseline projections depend on these estimates.
- **Agribusiness** — Input suppliers, grain handlers, processors, and transportation/logistics planning.
- **Researchers** — Agricultural economics, agronomy, climate/food-security research; the long time series supports trend and climate-impact analysis.
- **International bodies** — FAO, foreign governments, and global food-security monitors treat NASS estimates as the benchmark for U.S. supply.
- **Journalists and the public** — Food price and harvest reporting.

---

## 8. Public Benefits

1. **Market transparency and fairness** — Levels the information playing field between producers and buyers; simultaneous, equal public access is an explicit NASS hallmark.
2. **Policy infrastructure** — Underpins the farm safety net: crop insurance rate-setting, ARC/PLC program payments, ad hoc disaster aid, and the CBO farm-bill baseline.
3. **Food security and crisis response** — Early warning of shortfalls (droughts, floods) informs national and international response.
4. **Economic indicator value** — Feeds GDP components, inflation analysis, and trade projections.
5. **Scientific record** — A 160+ year climate-and-agriculture time series of exceptional longitudinal value.
6. **Taxpayer accountability** — Free, public-domain dissemination; methodology and quality measures (including standard errors) are published openly.

---

## 9. Preservation and Risk Considerations

**For preservationists and data librarians:**

- **Multiple redundant archives exist** — NASS, the National Agricultural Library (ESMIS), and Cornell Mann Library all hold runs; this redundancy is a strength, but the three holdings differ in completeness and format.
- **Format risks** — Historical issues exist as PDFs and plain text; the TXT files are the most preservation-friendly. Very early reports (pre-20th century) exist largely in print and scanned form, scattered across libraries and the National Archives (Record Group 355).
- **Vintage/revision preservation** — Because estimates are revised, preserving *each monthly issue* (not just annual finals) is essential for reconstructing what was known when — crucial for market-behavior and policy research.
- **API dependence** — Quick Stats is the primary machine-readable channel; it has no statutory permanence guarantee. Third-party mirrors of the bulk dumps (e.g., academic data libraries converting them to Parquet) already exist and should be encouraged.
- **Metadata** — ESMIS provides structured bibliographic metadata via its REST API, which is harvestable for repository ingest.

**Risks and threats (verify current status independently — this area changes quickly):**

- **Funding and staffing pressures** — NASS has faced repeated budget constraints; in recent years it has periodically announced **discontinuation or reduction of lower-priority reports and surveys** (and industry/commodity groups have publicly lobbied to restore them). Crop Production itself, as a market-sensitive principal report, is among the *least* likely to be cut — but the surveys that feed it (Objective Yield, county-level estimates) are where degradation would first appear.
- **Survey response rates** — Declining farmer response rates are a documented, long-running methodological concern affecting estimate quality.
- **Political independence** — Because the numbers move markets and drive program payments, the ASB's independence and the lockup system are deliberately insulated; any erosion of that insulation is a red flag for data-integrity watchdogs.
- **Website/system transitions** — NASS has publicly noted system updates that may interrupt website access; users are directed to ESMIS as a fallback — another reason multi-archive preservation matters.

---

## 10. Key Primary Sources for Further Research

- Report archive: `nass.usda.gov/Publications` and `esmis.nal.usda.gov/publication/crop-production`
- CRS Report R44814, *NASS and U.S. Crop Production Forecasts* (excellent on authority and methodology)
- NASS, *The Story of U.S. Agricultural Estimates* and *Safeguarding America's Agricultural Statistics* (official histories)
- 7 CFR § 2.68 (delegations); 7 U.S.C. §§ 476, 951, 2204, 2204g, 2276; CIPSEA (44 U.S.C. ch. 35, Title III of P.L. 115-435)
- National Archives, Records of NASS (Record Group 355) — full predecessor-agency lineage
- Quick Stats API documentation and bulk downloads at `nass.usda.gov`
- NASS "Methodology and Data Quality" publications issued alongside major releases

---

**Bottom line:** Your description checks out. The Crop Production report is one of the oldest, most legally protected, most economically consequential statistical products of the U.S. government — published under layered statutory authority by NASS's Agricultural Statistics Board, produced under extraordinary security procedures, freely available in human- and machine-readable forms, redundantly archived (NASS, NAL/ESMIS, Cornell), and foundational to markets, farm policy, food security, and a 160-year scientific record. The main preservation concerns are vintage/revision capture, longevity of the Quick Stats API channel, historical-format migration, and the funding/response-rate pressures that could degrade the surveys feeding it.

---

# Risk Assessment: USDA NASS "Crop Production" Report

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence considered:**
- *For No Known Issue*: Back issues remain publicly available through three redundant channels: the NASS publications archive, the National Agricultural Library's ESMIS archive (which has a documented public REST API), and Cornell Mann Library's USDA archive. Quick Stats continues to serve historical statistics down to county level. No evidence of removal or alteration of any prior-year Crop Production reports was found in news coverage, the Federal Register, or watchdog reporting (e.g., the American Statistical Association's 2025 "Nation's Data at Risk" review of NASS flags no deletion of historical products).
- *For Moderate/High*: The 2024 cancellation of County Estimates (later reversed) briefly threatened a gap year in county-level historical series, but NASS retroactively reinstated 2024 row-crop county estimates (March 2025 notice), closing the gap. The permanently skipped October 2025 issue (see §2) is a *missing* report, not a *removed* one, so it does not fit this category's definitions.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** Prior years and cycles remain accessible in original formats across multiple archives, with no known alterations. The only true gap (October 2025) is an absence of new data, not a removal of existing data.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence considered:**
- *For High Risk ("collection or publication skipped")*: During the 43-day federal government shutdown (Oct 1–mid-Nov 2025), NASS announced that the **October 9, 2025 Crop Production report "will not be released"** — a permanent skip of one monthly issue in the series. Six weeks of companion Crop Progress reports and three Cotton Ginnings reports were also permanently skipped (NASS notices, Oct 31 and Nov 19, 2025; Reuters, Oct 9 and Nov 13, 2025). This demonstrates the series can and does go dark during funding lapses, and that missed issues are not backfilled.
- *For Moderate Risk*: The November 2025 report was delayed (Nov 10 → Nov 14) but published, paired with WASDE; the December 2025-onward schedule resumed as normal, and 2026 monthly reports (June–September 2026 issues verified in the NASS publications listing) appear on time. No statutory publication deadline exists to be missed, and there is no indication of termination intent — indeed, Congress previously forced *reinstatement* of canceled NASS reports via appropriations language.
- *ICR status*: The core clearance, **OMB 0535-0002 (Field Crops Production), is Active with an expiration date of July 31, 2027** (reginfo.gov ICR ref. 202602-0535-001, approved with change 03/27/2026; earlier actions in Jan 2026 and July 2025). No lapse. This weighs against High.

**Selected level: High Risk (on the rubric's letter), with important context.** The rubric defines High Risk as including "collection or publication skipped" — and a full monthly issue was permanently skipped in October 2025. However, this was a one-time, government-wide appropriations lapse rather than an agency- or policy-driven termination; the series resumed within weeks, the ICR is active through mid-2027, and 2026 publication is on schedule. If the rubric user weighs *recurrence likelihood* rather than the literal event, Moderate is defensible — but the demonstrated fact that issues are skipped rather than backfilled during shutdowns, combined with recurring CR/shutdown risk in the current fiscal environment, justifies High under a preservation-minded reading.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence considered:**
- *For High Risk (actual reductions)*: The **Cotton Objective Yield Survey was discontinued (April 2024) and — unlike the July Cattle report and County Estimates — was not reinstated**, permanently removing the in-field measurement basis for cotton yield forecasts that feed the Crop Production report; cotton estimates now rely more heavily on farmer-reported data. Timeliness measurably degraded during the shutdown (October issue skipped; November delayed).
- *For Moderate Risk (emerging risk)*: Staff losses of 34–54% (see §5) with four of seven divisions led by acting directors; elimination of state/regional reports; the American Statistical Association rates NASS resources **"WEAK,"** warning that staff reductions impair methodological upkeep and that outdated IT cannot be modernized; long-running declines in survey response rates; and a planned multi-year consolidation of 12 regional offices into 5 hubs that historically correlates with further attrition. Core national/state granularity, monthly frequency, and lockup procedures for Crop Production itself remain intact as of late 2026.
- *For No Known Issue*: The report's core structure, crops covered, release timing (noon ET), and ASB review process are unchanged; the only recent questionnaire change was an *addition* (two sugarcane questions, per the Oct 2, 2026 Federal Register notice).

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** The report's core granularity, frequency, and (post-shutdown) timeliness are currently maintained, but there are concrete, documented erosions at the margins (loss of the Cotton Objective Yield input, the shutdown-era timeliness failure) and strong leading indicators (staffing, leadership vacancies, IT/methodology stagnation flagged by ASA) that degradation of the inputs to this dataset is emerging rather than merely hypothetical.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence considered:**
- *For No Known Issue*: Authority is explicit and layered: the Organic Act of 1862 (statistics as USDA's first duty), **7 U.S.C. § 2204** (cited in the current ICR as the collection authority), the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, commodity-specific statutes, and the formal delegation at **7 CFR § 2.68** directing the NASS Administrator to "prepare crop and livestock estimates… reports of the Agricultural Statistics Board." The ICR's own "Need and Use" statement affirms that **the Secretary uses these estimates to administer farm program legislation and import/export programs** — a clear programmatic use. No alternative collection can substitute: the official ASB estimates are the legally embedded benchmark for WASDE, CBO baselines, crop insurance, and program payments, and private estimates cannot replicate the mandatory, confidential, probability-survey infrastructure.
- *For Moderate/High*: No serious evidence. One nuance: when NASS cut County Estimates in 2024, it argued RMA uses its own internal data — a partial-substitute argument at the county level, but not for the Crop Production report itself.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** This is among the most statutorily grounded, program-embedded statistical products in the federal government, with no viable substitute collection.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence considered:**
- *For High Risk*: Multiple independent measurements exceed the 40% threshold or approach it: the **USDA OIG (Dec. 2025) documents NASS losing 275 of 805 employees (34%)** between Jan 12 and Jun 14, 2025; press analyses put it at **37% — "the largest percentage of any [USDA] agency"** (WPR/HPPR/Nebraska Public Media, Feb. 2026); the **American Statistical Association estimates 41% of FY24 staff lost**, and an Agri-Pulse-cited analysis shows FTEs falling from **839 (FY23) to 389 (FY26), a 54% decline**. Leadership has been hollowed out: as of Nov. 2025 the associate administrator is acting, multiple administrator's-office units have acting or no directors, and four of seven divisions have acting directors (ASA). This fits "40% or more of staff lost" and "leadership removed."
- *For Moderate Risk*: Only if one credits the OIG's narrower 34% (through June 2025) figure and excludes leadership hollowing — but subsequent DRP separations after the OIG window push the true figure higher, and the FY26 budget request (495 staff) locks in the reduced level.
- *Mitigants*: The FY26 President's Budget holds staffing roughly flat at the reduced level rather than cutting further, and Congress has previously restored funding for canceled reports.

**Selected level: High Risk.** Even the most conservative official figure (34%, USDA OIG) sits at the top of the Moderate band; independent estimates (41%, ASA; 54% FTE decline over three years) exceed the 40% High threshold, and the acting-leadership situation independently satisfies the "leadership removed" criterion.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence considered:**
- *For No Known Issue*: Since January 2025, there is **no documented change to what the Crop Production report collects or publishes**: no Presidential-Action-driven ICR for these surveys, no negative policy note on the report's pages, and no verified statement by administration officials targeting crop production estimates (unlike, e.g., the BLS commissioner firing). The only ICR changes are routine (a confidentiality-pledge update requested by OMB; added sugarcane questions).
- *For Moderate Risk*: The administration has demonstrated willingness to alter NASS's portfolio on efficiency grounds — the **Aug. 28, 2025 discontinuation of the Agricultural Labor and Mink surveys was explicitly framed as a Paperwork Reduction Act/efficiency action**; the **July 24, 2025 USDA Reorganization Plan (SM 1078-015)** relocates NASS staff and consolidates its 12 regions into 5 hubs; and NASS already canceled and restored reports once in this budget cycle, showing collection decisions are actively being revisited. These are pending/in-progress changes and signals consistent with "statements… suggesting a change is being considered or planned" at the agency level, though not aimed at this specific dataset.
- *For High Risk*: Not supported — no Presidential-Action ICR or directive targets Crop Production.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** Crop Production itself is untouched by administration policy to date, and its market sensitivity makes direct targeting unlikely. But the agency producing it is undergoing an administration-directed reorganization and efficiency-driven portfolio pruning, which constitutes proposed/pending changes to the environment that determines what is collected and published — enough to move this dataset out of "No notable changes."

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue** — full backfile intact across three redundant archives.
- **Future Data Availability: High Risk** — one monthly issue (Oct 2025) permanently skipped during the shutdown; series since resumed and ICR active through July 2027, but the skip-and-don't-backfill precedent plus recurring funding-lapse risk satisfies the rubric's High definition.
- **Data Quality: Moderate Risk** — core report maintained, but a permanent input loss (Cotton Objective Yield), demonstrated timeliness failure, and staffing-driven methodological erosion flagged by ASA.
- **Statutory Context: No Known Issue** — explicit statutory authority (7 U.S.C. § 2204; 7 CFR § 2.68), embedded in farm-program implementation, no substitutes.
- **Staffing and Funding: High Risk** — 34–54% staff loss depending on measure, exceeding/nearing the 40% threshold; leadership positions vacant or acting.
- **Policy: Moderate Risk** — no direct action against this dataset, but administration-driven reorganization and efficiency-based survey discontinuations at NASS signal active reconsideration of the agency's portfolio.

**Overall interpretation:** The dataset's greatest near-term vulnerability is not malice or statutory weakness — it is **capacity**. A statutory fortress (§4) is being defended by a shrinking garrison (§5), and the October 2025 skip (§2) proves the publication pipeline breaks under fiscal stress. For preservationists, the practical priorities follow directly: mirror every monthly issue as it drops (including TXT/ZIP formats and Quick Stats vintages), verify holdings for the missing October 2025 cycle in derivative products, and monitor the NASS newsroom's "Notices" page — where both the 2024 cancellations and the 2025 reinstatements were first announced — as the earliest-warning channel for any future changes.
